ram_memory.title: RAM (Random Access Memory)
ram_memory.definition: High-speed volatile semiconductor memory utilized by the processor to hold active program instructions, operating system kernel routines, and working data sets while powered.
ram_memory.context: Loses all stored data instantly when electrical power is removed or interrupted during a reboot.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.1: Resolve problems with motherboard, RAM, CPU, and power

non_volatile_storage.title: Non-Volatile Storage
non_volatile_storage.definition: Secondary data persistence hardware such as solid-state drives, magnetic hard disks, or flash memory that retains stored binary data without continuous electrical power.
non_volatile_storage.context: Houses operating system installations, permanent application binaries, user documents, and system configuration registries across reboots.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.2: Troubleshoot storage drives and RAID arrays

post_routine.title: POST (Power-On Self-Test)
post_routine.definition: An initial diagnostic sequence executed by system firmware (BIOS or UEFI) immediately upon startup to verify and initialize core hardware components before loading the OS.
post_routine.context: Validates CPU registers, system memory integrity, display controllers, and bus interfaces, halting or emitting diagnostic beep/hex codes if essential hardware fails.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.1: Motherboard and boot sequence troubleshooting

network_interface_card.title: NIC (Network Interface Card)
network_interface_card.definition: A hardware expansion card or onboard controller that implements physical Layer 1 signaling and Layer 2 data link framing to connect a computer to a local network.
network_interface_card.context: Converts internal digital system bus transactions into serialized electrical, optical, or radio transmissions across physical network media.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 2.1: Compare and contrast network hardware devices

mac_address.title: MAC Address
mac_address.definition: A globally unique 48-bit physical identifier burned into the firmware of a network interface card by the manufacturer to facilitate Layer 2 frame delivery on local Ethernet segments.
mac_address.context: Operates exclusively within a single local broadcast domain, remaining unchanged across networks and never routing across internet boundaries.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 2.4: Summarize basic networking concepts

ip_address.title: IP Address
ip_address.definition: A logical 32-bit (IPv4) or 128-bit (IPv6) numerical identifier assigned to a network interface to enable routable packet delivery across interconnected Layer 3 network domains.
ip_address.context: Assigned dynamically via DHCP or statically by network administrators, reflecting the host's topological location on a logical subnet rather than its physical hardware identity.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 2.6: Configure basic networking host settings

post_code.title: POST Code
post_code.definition: A hexadecimal diagnostic code output by system firmware during the Power-On Self-Test to identify hardware initialization progress and specific subsystem failures.
post_code.context: Displayed on onboard seven-segment displays or port 80h diagnostic cards before video display drivers initialize.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.1: Given a scenario, resolve problems with motherboard, RAM, CPU, and power

rs232_serial.title: RS-232 Serial
rs232_serial.definition: A legacy standard for serial binary data transmission between data terminal equipment (DTE) and data circuit-terminating equipment (DCE), commonly utilizing DB-9 connectors.
rs232_serial.context: Frequently deployed in rugged industrial equipment, automated weighing scales, barcode scanners, and network management consoles.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.4: Given a scenario, troubleshoot and resolve peripheral and display problems

baud_rate.title: Baud Rate
baud_rate.definition: The rate at which signal states or electrical symbols change per second along a serial communication channel, requiring matching transmitter and receiver clocking.
baud_rate.context: In binary serial links, a mismatch between sender and receiver baud rates creates severe frame desynchronization and unreadable garbled characters.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.4: Troubleshoot peripheral interfaces and communications

multimeter.title: Multimeter
multimeter.definition: A handheld electronic test instrument used to measure electrical voltage (AC/DC), resistance (ohms), and current (amperes) across hardware circuits.
multimeter.context: Used by technicians to test power supply rail tolerances (+12V, +5V, +3.3V) and trace broken or grounded conductors.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.1: Power supply troubleshooting and voltage rail verification

continuity_test.title: Continuity Test
continuity_test.definition: An electrical test performed with a multimeter to verify an unbroken, low-resistance conduction path between two points in a circuit or conductor.
continuity_test.context: Produces an audible tone when a continuous circuit exists, isolating severed copper traces, short circuits to chassis ground, or broken cable cores.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.1: Motherboard and cabling fault isolation

dip_switch.title: DIP Switch
dip_switch.definition: Dual in-line package manual electrical switches mounted on a printed circuit board to configure hardware parameters and operational modes directly.
dip_switch.context: Commonly used on embedded motherboards, industrial scales, and expansion cards to configure baud rates, hardware addresses, or bus timings without software.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) Objective 3.1: Motherboard configuration and embedded jumpers

troubleshooting_methodology.title: Troubleshooting Methodology
troubleshooting_methodology.definition: The standardized six-step diagnostic framework used to identify, isolate, resolve, and document computing failures.
troubleshooting_methodology.context: On the desk, it is the discipline of binary search: eliminating half the potential failure domains with every test before touching settings.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1102) Objective 1.4

safe_mode.title: Safe Mode
safe_mode.definition: A diagnostic boot state that loads Windows with a minimal set of essential drivers and system services.
safe_mode.context: Used to determine whether a system crash or hang originates in base operating system files or third-party software and drivers.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1102) Objective 1.4

event_viewer.title: Event Viewer
event_viewer.definition: A Microsoft Management Console snap-in that logs system, application, and security messages, errors, and audit events.
event_viewer.context: Provides authoritative timestamps and error codes (such as Event IDs 1000 and 41) that distinguish software crashes from kernel power cuts.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1102) Objective 1.4

clean_boot.title: Clean Boot
clean_boot.definition: An operating system startup state achieved by disabling all non-Microsoft background services and startup applications.
clean_boot.context: Isolates third-party software conflicts through systematic binary elimination without disabling essential Windows core functions.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1102) Objective 1.4

device_driver.title: Device Driver
device_driver.definition: A specialized software program that allows the operating system kernel to communicate with and control physical hardware components.
device_driver.context: Corrupted or mismatched graphics drivers running in kernel space can lock the entire desktop when applications invoke hardware acceleration.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1102) Objective 1.1

bitlocker_recovery.title: BitLocker Recovery Key
bitlocker_recovery.definition: A 48-digit numerical password required to unlock a BitLocker-encrypted volume when platform configuration registers (PCRs) detect hardware or firmware changes.
bitlocker_recovery.context: Stored in Active Directory or Azure AD and released to users only after out-of-band identity verification to prevent unauthorized data access.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1102) Objective 2.8

apipa_address.title: APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing)
apipa_address.definition: A link-local IPv4 address autoconfiguration mechanism where a host assigns itself an address in the 169.254.0.1 to 169.254.255.254 range when a DHCP server fails to respond.
apipa_address.context: Indicates that physical Layer 1 and 2 links are operational, but DHCP DORA broadcast discovery failed to cross the local broadcast domain or VLAN trunk.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — IPv4 addressing and link-local autoconfiguration
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 4.1 — Troubleshooting IP configuration and DHCP failures

subnet_mask.title: Subnet Mask
subnet_mask.definition: A 32-bit bitmask that delineates the network prefix from the host identifier within an IPv4 address to determine whether a destination sits on the local or a remote subnet.
subnet_mask.context: Applied via bitwise logical ANDing by the host operating system to determine whether an IP packet can be delivered directly via local ARP or must be forwarded to the default gateway.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — IPv4 subnetting and classless inter-domain routing
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 1.4 — Network addressing and subnet masks

default_gateway.title: Default Gateway
default_gateway.definition: A Layer 3 router interface on the local subnet to which a host forwards IP packets destined for remote networks outside its own broadcast domain.
default_gateway.context: Hosts resolve the default gateway's Layer 2 MAC address via ARP and encapsulate outbound remote packets in Ethernet frames directed to that router interface.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — Default gateways and Layer 3 routing primitives
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 4.1 — Troubleshooting routing and gateway reachability

arp_cache.title: ARP Cache
arp_cache.definition: A volatile local operating system table that maps Layer 3 IPv4 addresses to their corresponding Layer 2 physical MAC addresses for hosts on the local network segment.
arp_cache.context: Inspected via `arp -a`, entries expire dynamically to reflect network changes, but can be poisoned or cause flapping during duplicate IP address conflicts.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — Address Resolution Protocol and MAC binding
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 4.1 — Diagnosing duplicate IPs and Layer 2 flapping

broadcast_domain.title: Broadcast Domain
broadcast_domain.definition: A logical division of a computer network within which all connected nodes can reach each other by Layer 2 broadcast transmission.
broadcast_domain.context: Bounded by Layer 3 routers and separated by VLAN configurations on switches; DHCP Discover and ARP request broadcasts are confined within this boundary.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — Broadcast domains, collision domains, and VLAN segmentation
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 2.1 — Switching features and VLAN trunking

dhcp_dora.title: DHCP DORA Process
dhcp_dora.definition: The four-step client-server state machine (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) used by Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol to automatically lease an IP address and network configuration to a client.
dhcp_dora.context: Operates over UDP ports 67 (server) and 68 (client); requires a DHCP relay agent (ip helper-address) on routers when clients and DHCP servers occupy different broadcast domains.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — DHCP operation and address allocation
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 1.4 — Network services and dynamic configuration

split_dns.title: Split-Horizon DNS
split_dns.definition: A domain name system architecture where internal and external queries for the same domain receive different IP address answers based on the client's network vantage point.
split_dns.context: Resolves private RFC 1918 addresses to hosts on the corporate LAN while providing external gateways or public landing pages to queries originating from the public internet.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.5 — DNS services and architectures
CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Domain 2.5 — Network architecture and segmentation

dns_leak.title: DNS Leak
dns_leak.definition: A network configuration flaw where DNS requests from a VPN-connected host are inadvertently transmitted across unencrypted local network adapters to a public resolver rather than through the secure VPN tunnel.
dns_leak.context: Occurs frequently in split-tunneling VPN configurations when client multi-homed resolution logic prioritizes the local physical gateway over the virtual tunnel adapter.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 4.2 — Troubleshooting remote access and VPN issues
CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Domain 2.5 — Secure remote access configurations

hosts_file.title: Hosts File
hosts_file.definition: An operating system text file that provides static, local mappings between hostnames and IP addresses, evaluated prior to querying external DNS servers.
hosts_file.context: Located at C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts on Windows systems, often modified for temporary testing or exploited by malware to hijack web traffic.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 4.1 — Network troubleshooting tools and client resolver sequence
CompTIA A+ Core 2 220-1102 — Windows configuration and security files

recursive_resolver.title: Recursive Resolver
recursive_resolver.definition: A DNS server that accepts queries from client stub resolvers and traverses the hierarchical DNS tree to obtain and return the definitive answer to the requester.
recursive_resolver.context: Caches resolution answers locally according to record time-to-live values to accelerate subsequent queries from corporate workstations.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.5 — DNS hierarchy and query flow

dns_ttl.title: DNS TTL (Time-to-Live)
dns_ttl.definition: A numeric value configured in a DNS record that dictates the number of seconds a recursive resolver or client cache is permitted to store the record before requesting a fresh query.
dns_ttl.context: Lower values enable rapid zone updates during server migrations but increase server query load, while higher values prolong resolution delays during cutovers.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.5 — DNS record parameters and caching

cname_record.title: CNAME Record
cname_record.definition: A Canonical Name record in DNS that aliases one domain name or subdomain to another fully qualified domain name rather than directly pointing to an IP address.
cname_record.context: Requires the resolving client to perform an additional lookup step to resolve the canonical target name, widely used for cloud service and CDN routing.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.5 — Common DNS record types

tcp_handshake.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
tcp_handshake.definition: The connection establishment process in Transmission Control Protocol where a client and server exchange SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK packets to synchronize sequence numbers and allocate resources before data transfer.
tcp_handshake.context: Guarantees reliable bidirectional delivery and sequence synchronization; if the SYN packet drops or encounters no listening service, data exchange cannot begin.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.1 — OSI and TCP/IP transport models
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 1.1 — Network protocols and TCP connection establishment

socket_state.title: Socket State
socket_state.definition: The operational status of a network communication endpoint within the TCP state machine, such as LISTENING, ESTABLISHED, CLOSE_WAIT, or TIME_WAIT.
socket_state.context: Inspected via diagnostic utilities such as netstat or ss to verify whether a server daemon is awaiting connections or whether client sockets are stalled in teardown.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — Ports, protocols, and socket states
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 4.1 — Troubleshooting transport layer connectivity

listening_port.title: Listening Port
listening_port.definition: A network port bound by a background server daemon or application process configured to accept incoming connection requests from remote clients.
listening_port.context: Represented in operating system tables as 0.0.0.0:<port> or [::]:<port> in the LISTENING state; connections to unbound ports are actively refused or dropped.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — Network services and listening ports
CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Domain 2.1 — Port security and service exposure

reset_packet.title: TCP Reset (RST)
reset_packet.definition: A TCP control segment with the RST flag asserted, sent by a host to abruptly terminate a connection or actively reject an inbound packet directed to an unbound port.
reset_packet.context: Causes client applications to report 'Connection refused', confirming that the physical link and routing are functional but no listening daemon accepted the SYN packet.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 4.1 — Network troubleshooting and packet analysis
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 4.1 — Diagnosing TCP connection rejections and resets

ephemeral_port.title: Ephemeral Port
ephemeral_port.definition: A dynamic, short-lived transport layer port assigned automatically by a client operating system from a high-numbered range (typically 49152 to 65535) to identify an outbound session.
ephemeral_port.context: Combined with the client IP, destination IP, and destination port to forge the unique 4-tuple socket identifier required for bidirectional TCP session tracking.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 — Port ranges and ephemeral dynamic assignment
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 1.4 — Transport layer addressing and port allocations

port_exhaustion.title: Ephemeral Port Exhaustion
port_exhaustion.definition: A state where a client operating system depletes its entire range of dynamic outbound ports, preventing any new outbound network connections from establishing.
port_exhaustion.context: Frequently triggered by high-frequency scripts or automated backup jobs that rapidly open and close connections, stranding thousands of sockets in the TIME_WAIT state.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 4.1 — Diagnosing socket and resource exhaustion
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 4.1 — Troubleshooting network performance and socket bottlenecks

authentication.title: Authentication
authentication.definition: Proving a claimed identity is genuine — typically with something you know, have, or are.
authentication.context: Distinct from authorization (what you may do after you prove who you are).
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — authentication methods / identity

authorization.title: Authorization
authorization.definition: Deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed to do (permissions, roles, resources).
authorization.context: Often shortened to authz; not the same as authentication.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — authorization / access control

accounting.title: Accounting
accounting.definition: Recording what an authenticated identity did — logs, sessions, and audit trails (the third A in AAA).
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — AAA / auditing

identification.title: Identification
identification.definition: Claiming an identity (username, badge ID, email) before authentication proves it.
identification.context: Saying who you are is not the same as proving it.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — identity concepts

something_you_know.title: Something you know
something_you_know.definition: Knowledge factor — password, PIN, passphrase, or security question answer.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — authentication factors

something_you_have.title: Something you have
something_you_have.definition: Possession factor — phone authenticator, hardware token, security key, or smart card.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — authentication factors

something_you_are.title: Something you are
something_you_are.definition: Inherence factor — biometrics such as fingerprint, face, or iris.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — authentication factors / biometrics

somewhere_you_are.title: Somewhere you are
somewhere_you_are.definition: Location / context attribute — geo, network segment, or trusted site used as an additional signal.
somewhere_you_are.context: Often treated as a contextual attribute rather than a classic factor.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — authentication attributes / context

single_factor.title: Single-factor authentication
single_factor.definition: Using only one authentication factor type. Password plus PIN is still single-factor — both are something you know.
single_factor.context: Two knowledge secrets do not equal MFA.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MFA vs single-factor

mfa.title: Multifactor authentication (MFA)
mfa.definition: Requiring two or more different factor types (know / have / are) before access is granted.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — multifactor authentication

password.title: Password
password.definition: A secret string used as a knowledge factor for authentication.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — password security

pin.title: PIN
pin.definition: Personal identification number — a short numeric knowledge factor, not a second factor type when paired with a password.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — authentication factors

passphrase.title: Passphrase
passphrase.definition: A longer memorable phrase used as a password; length often beats dense complexity rules.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — password security

password_length.title: Password length
password_length.definition: How many characters a password has; modern guidance prioritizes sufficient length over ornate complexity alone.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — password best practices

password_complexity.title: Password complexity
password_complexity.definition: Rules requiring mixed character classes (upper, lower, digit, symbol). Helpful, but length and uniqueness matter more.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — password best practices

password_reuse.title: Password reuse
password_reuse.definition: Using the same password across systems or recycling recent passwords — spreads breach impact.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — password best practices

password_expiration.title: Password expiration
password_expiration.definition: Forcing periodic password changes on a schedule. Modern guidance often prefers change-on-compromise over short expiry cycles.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — password policies

password_age.title: Password age
password_age.definition: How long the current password has been in use; tracked so policy can enforce maximum age or detect stale secrets.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — password policies

password_manager.title: Password manager
password_manager.definition: Tool that stores unique strong passwords (and often autofills them) so users need not reuse secrets.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — password security / credential management

passwordless.title: Passwordless
passwordless.definition: Authentication that replaces passwords with possession and/or biometrics (e.g. security keys, passkeys, device unlock).
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — authentication methods

soft_token.title: Soft token
soft_token.definition: Software-based possession factor — typically an authenticator app generating one-time codes.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MFA methods / tokens

hard_token.title: Hard token
hard_token.definition: Hardware possession factor — a dedicated device that generates or stores one-time codes or cryptographic keys.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MFA methods / tokens

security_key.title: Security key
security_key.definition: Hardware authenticator (often USB/NFC) that proves possession via cryptography — phishing-resistant when used as a second factor or passwordless.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MFA / hardware authenticators

totp.title: TOTP
totp.definition: Time-based one-time password — short codes from a shared secret that rotate on a clock (common in authenticator apps).
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MFA / OTP

sms_otp.title: SMS OTP
sms_otp.definition: One-time code delivered by text message. Better than password alone, but weaker than app or hardware factors (SIM swap, interception).
sms_otp.context: Acceptable stopgap; prefer app or security key when policy allows.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MFA methods / SMS risks

push_notification.title: Push notification (MFA)
push_notification.definition: Approve/deny prompt sent to a registered device as a possession check.
push_notification.context: Convenient, but users can be trained into tapping Approve under fatigue or social pressure.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MFA methods

biometrics.title: Biometrics (door)
biometrics.definition: Unlocking with something you are — fingerprint, face, iris — often combined with a badge or PIN.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — biometrics

sso.title: Single sign-on (SSO)
sso.definition: Authenticate once to an identity provider, then access multiple apps without separate logins for each.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — SSO / federation

federation.title: Federation
federation.definition: Trust relationship that lets one organization's identity provider assert identity to another system's service provider.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — federation

saml.title: SAML
saml.definition: Security Assertion Markup Language — common enterprise SSO protocol exchanging XML assertions between IdP and service.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — federation protocols (SAML)

oauth.title: OAuth
oauth.definition: Authorization framework often used so apps get limited access tokens without sharing the user's password (desk tickets may say 'OAuth SSO' loosely).
oauth.context: At the desk: usually means the app is wired to the company IdP for sign-in / consent, not a password paste.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — OAuth / federation-related access

least_privilege.title: Least privilege
least_privilege.definition: Grant only the access needed for the job — nothing extra 'just in case.'
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — least privilege

rbac.title: Role-based access control (RBAC)
rbac.definition: Assign permissions to roles (job functions), then assign users to roles — instead of one-off rights per person.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — access control models (RBAC)

account_lockout.title: Account lockout
account_lockout.definition: Temporarily disabling an account after too many failed authentication attempts to slow password guessing.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — account policies / lockout

provisioning.title: Provisioning
provisioning.definition: Creating accounts and assigning access when someone joins or changes roles.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — account management / provisioning

deprovisioning.title: Deprovisioning
deprovisioning.definition: Removing or disabling accounts and access when someone leaves or no longer needs them.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — account management / offboarding

privileged_access.title: Privileged access
privileged_access.definition: Elevated rights (admin, root, domain) that can change systems or read sensitive data — tightly controlled.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — privileged access management concepts

pam.title: Privileged access management (PAM)
pam.definition: Controls for privileged accounts — vaulting shared secrets, just-in-time elevation, and session oversight.
pam.context: Desk-level: admins check out a vaulted password or request temporary elevation instead of sharing a sticky.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — privileged access management

help_desk.title: Help desk
help_desk.definition: Front-line IT support that takes tickets, coaches users, and escalates security signals.

ticket.title: Ticket
ticket.definition: Tracked support request — the work unit the desk opens, updates, and closes.

identity_provider.title: Identity provider (IdP)
identity_provider.definition: System that authenticates users and issues assertions/tokens other apps trust (the 'sign in with company' brain).

authenticator_app.title: Authenticator app
authenticator_app.definition: Phone or desktop app that holds soft-token secrets and shows rotating TOTP codes (or push prompts).

backup_codes.title: Backup codes
backup_codes.definition: One-time recovery codes issued at MFA enrollment for when the phone or token is unavailable.

mfa_fatigue.title: MFA fatigue
mfa_fatigue.definition: Attack or habit where a user is spammed with push prompts until they approve one without thinking.

shoulder_surfing.title: Shoulder surfing
shoulder_surfing.definition: Watching someone type a PIN, password, or badge code from nearby — eyes as the attack tool.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — shoulder surfing

shared_admin_account.title: Shared admin account
shared_admin_account.definition: One privileged login used by multiple people — breaks accountability and complicates offboarding.

break_glass.title: Break-glass account
break_glass.definition: Emergency privileged account for outages when normal MFA/IdP paths fail — tightly vaulted and audited.

just_in_time.title: Just-in-time (JIT) access
just_in_time.definition: Temporary elevation granted only when needed, then revoked — instead of standing admin rights.

vaulting.title: Credential vaulting
vaulting.definition: Storing privileged passwords in a controlled vault with checkout, rotation, and audit — not a shared spreadsheet.

offboarding.title: Offboarding
offboarding.definition: HR/IT process when someone leaves — disable accounts, reclaim devices, and strip residual access.

encryption.title: Encryption
encryption.definition: Transforming readable data into ciphertext so only parties with the right key can recover the original.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — encryption

hashing.title: Hashing
hashing.definition: One-way fingerprint of data — fixed-length digest used to check integrity, not to hide and later reveal secrets.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — hashing

encoding.title: Encoding
encoding.definition: Reversible representation change (like Base64) for transport or display — not confidentiality; anyone can decode.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — encoding vs encryption

obfuscation.title: Obfuscation
obfuscation.definition: Making something harder to read or understand without providing real cryptographic strength by itself.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — obfuscation

steganography.title: Steganography
steganography.definition: Hiding a message inside other media (image, audio, file) so the secret's existence is less obvious.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — steganography

plaintext.title: Plaintext
plaintext.definition: Data in readable form before encryption — the thing you are trying not to leave lying around.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — plaintext / ciphertext

ciphertext.title: Ciphertext
ciphertext.definition: Encrypted output — unreadable without the correct cryptographic key.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — plaintext / ciphertext

symmetric.title: Symmetric encryption
symmetric.definition: Same key encrypts and decrypts — fast for bulk data; key distribution is the hard part.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — symmetric encryption

asymmetric.title: Asymmetric encryption
asymmetric.definition: Key pair model — public key encrypts or verifies; private key decrypts or signs.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — asymmetric / public-key cryptography

public_key.title: Public key
public_key.definition: Shareable half of a key pair — used to encrypt to someone or verify their digital signature.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — public/private keys

private_key.title: Private key
private_key.definition: Secret half of a key pair — decrypts or signs; must stay protected or the trust story collapses.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — public/private keys

key_exchange.title: Key exchange
key_exchange.definition: Method for agreeing on a shared secret over an untrusted channel (often using asymmetric math so symmetric keys can follow).
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — key exchange

perfect_forward_secrecy.title: Perfect forward secrecy
perfect_forward_secrecy.definition: Property where past session keys stay safe even if a long-term private key is later stolen — ephemeral session secrets.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — perfect forward secrecy / PFS

digital_signature.title: Digital signature
digital_signature.definition: Private-key operation that proves origin and integrity of data — verifiers use the matching public key.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — digital signatures

non_repudiation.title: Non-repudiation
non_repudiation.definition: Difficulty denying you signed or sent something when a valid signature and key custody support the claim.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — non-repudiation

salting.title: Salting
salting.definition: Random value mixed into password hashing so identical passwords do not produce identical hashes.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — salting

integrity.title: Integrity
integrity.definition: Assurance that data has not been altered — often checked with hashes or signatures.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — integrity

pki.title: PKI
pki.definition: Public key infrastructure — the people, policies, and systems that issue and manage certificates and trust.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — PKI

certificate.title: Client/server certificate (Wi-Fi)
certificate.definition: Credential material used in enterprise Wi-Fi so clients can verify the real RADIUS/network and not a twin.

ca.title: Certificate authority (CA)
ca.definition: Trusted issuer that signs certificates after validating identity — the root of many trust decisions.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — certificate authority

intermediate_ca.title: Intermediate CA
intermediate_ca.definition: CA beneath the root that issues end-entity certificates — keeps the root offline and the chain manageable.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — intermediate CA / certificate chain

csr.title: CSR
csr.definition: Certificate signing request — package with your public key and identity details sent to a CA for signing.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — CSR

self_signed.title: Self-signed certificate
self_signed.definition: Certificate signed by its own key instead of a trusted CA — fine for lab toys, scary in production browsers.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — self-signed certificates

expired_cert.title: Expired certificate
expired_cert.definition: Certificate past its validity dates — browsers and clients correctly refuse or warn because trust has a calendar.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — certificate expiration / validation

certificate_pinning.title: Certificate / public-key pinning
certificate_pinning.definition: Client remembers an expected cert or key and rejects surprises — stronger against some MitM, brittle when pins go stale.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — certificate pinning

tls.title: TLS
tls.definition: Transport Layer Security — the encryption layer that wraps many application protocols into secure versions.

key_escrow.title: Key escrow
key_escrow.definition: Storing decryption keys with a trusted third party so data can be recovered under policy — powerful and controversial.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — key escrow

hsm.title: HSM
hsm.definition: Hardware security module — hardened device that generates and protects keys so private material rarely leaves the box.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — HSM

key_management.title: Key management
key_management.definition: Lifecycle of creating, storing, rotating, revoking, and destroying cryptographic keys without leaking them.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — key management

certificate_chain.title: Certificate chain
certificate_chain.definition: Path from end-entity certificate through intermediate CA(s) to a trusted root — missing links break trust.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — certificate chain / chaining

wildcard_cert.title: Wildcard certificate
wildcard_cert.definition: Certificate that covers many hostnames under one domain (like *.example.com) — convenient, broader blast radius if stolen.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — wildcard certificates

browser_padlock.title: Browser padlock
browser_padlock.definition: UI hint that the page is using HTTPS/TLS — not a guarantee the site is honest, only that the channel looks encrypted to a trusted name.

cert_warning.title: Certificate warning dialog
cert_warning.definition: Browser interstitial when TLS validation fails — expired, name mismatch, untrusted issuer, or broken chain.

trust_store.title: Trust store
trust_store.definition: Collection of root/intermediate CAs the OS or browser trusts by default — the quiet list behind the padlock.

base64.title: Base64
base64.definition: Common encoding that turns binary into ASCII-safe text — looks 'scrambled' but is not encryption.

https.title: HTTPS (443/TCP)
https.definition: HTTP secured with TLS. Default for modern web traffic.
https.context: Use instead of cleartext HTTP for any page that takes credentials or personal data.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — implement secure protocols (web)

soc.title: SOC
soc.definition: Security operations center — team that monitors alerts, investigates wireless attacks, and coordinates response.

event.title: Event
event.definition: An observable occurrence in a system or network — a login, alert, crash, or odd ticket — that may or may not be a security problem.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — events vs incidents

security_incident.title: Security incident
security_incident.definition: A violation or imminent threat of violation of security policy, acceptable use, or standard security practices — not every scary ticket qualifies.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — security incidents

escalation.title: Escalation
escalation.definition: Handing an issue to a higher or more specialized team when criteria are met — with clean facts, not a Slack panic dump.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — escalation

first_responder.title: First responder
first_responder.definition: First person or team to touch an incident — at many orgs the help desk is that first touch and must preserve options for IR.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — first responders

csirt.title: CSIRT / IR team
csirt.definition: Computer Security Incident Response Team (or equivalent IR team) — specialists who own analysis, forensics coordination, and incident command after escalation.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — CSIRT / incident response team

chain_of_custody.title: Chain of custody
chain_of_custody.definition: Documented control of evidence — who had it, when, and what changed — so findings stay credible and you do not casually wipe a laptop IR still needs.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — chain of custody

ioc.title: Indicators of compromise (IoC)
ioc.definition: Observable clues that a system or account may be compromised — hashes, domains, odd processes, weird outbound traffic.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — indicators of compromise / malicious activity

quarantine.title: Quarantine
quarantine.definition: Holding suspicious mail or files away from the inbox so users cannot open them until reviewed.

isolation.title: Isolation
isolation.definition: Separating a system from the network or peers to stop spread — pull the cable, disable Wi-Fi, or VLAN-park the host.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — isolation

need_to_know.title: Need-to-know
need_to_know.definition: Principle of sharing incident details only with people who require them to act — not blasting the whole company Slack.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — need-to-know / least privilege of information

malware.title: Malware
malware.definition: Malicious software — any program designed to harm, spy, extort, or take control of a system.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — malware

virus.title: Virus
virus.definition: Malware that attaches to files or programs and spreads when the host file runs or is shared.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — virus

worm.title: Worm
worm.definition: Self-replicating malware that spreads across networks without needing a user to open a file each time.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — worm

trojan.title: Trojan
trojan.definition: Malware disguised as something useful or expected so the user installs it willingly.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — trojan

ransomware.title: Ransomware
ransomware.definition: Malware that encrypts systems or data and demands payment; internet-exposed remote desktop is a common entry.

crypto_malware.title: Crypto-malware
crypto_malware.definition: Malware that encrypts files or volumes so victims cannot use their data without a key the attacker controls.
crypto_malware.context: Often the technical engine inside a ransomware incident.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — crypto-malware / ransomware

spyware.title: Spyware
spyware.definition: Malware that secretly collects information about users, systems, or activity and sends it to an attacker.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — spyware

adware.title: Adware
adware.definition: Unwanted software that pushes ads, redirects browsing, or tracks habits for advertising — often bundled with free installs.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — adware

keylogger.title: Keylogger
keylogger.definition: Software or hardware that records keystrokes to steal passwords, messages, or other typed secrets.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — keylogger

rootkit.title: Rootkit
rootkit.definition: Malware that hides deep in the system (often kernel-level) to conceal processes, files, or persistence from normal tools.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — rootkit

bot.title: Bot
bot.definition: A compromised device under remote attacker control, waiting for commands.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — bots / botnets

botnet.title: Botnet
botnet.definition: A network of bots controlled together — used for spam, DDoS, crypto-mining, or further compromise.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — botnet

logic_bomb.title: Logic bomb
logic_bomb.definition: Malicious code that sits dormant until a condition or date triggers it (fire after layoff, delete after deadline).
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — logic bomb

fileless.title: Fileless malware
fileless.definition: Attacks that run in memory or abuse built-in tools so little or no new malware file lands on disk.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — fileless malware

pups.title: PUPs (potentially unwanted programs)
pups.definition: Software users may have 'agreed' to install that is unwanted, deceptive, or risky — toolbars, bundles, junk helpers.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — PUPs / potentially unwanted programs

backdoor.title: Backdoor
backdoor.definition: A hidden way into a system that bypasses normal authentication — planted by malware or a malicious insider.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — backdoor

rat.title: Remote access Trojan (RAT)
rat.definition: A trojan that gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim machine.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — RAT / remote access trojan

dropper.title: Dropper
dropper.definition: A small malicious program whose job is to deliver and install other malware payloads.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — dropper / malware delivery

payload.title: Payload
payload.definition: The harmful action malware is built to perform once it runs — encrypt, spy, open a shell, join a botnet.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — malware payload

cryptojacking.title: Cryptojacking
cryptojacking.definition: Hijacking a system's CPU/GPU to mine cryptocurrency for the attacker without consent.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — cryptomalware / cryptojacking

command_and_control.title: Command and control (C2)
command_and_control.definition: The channel attackers use to send orders to compromised hosts and pull stolen data back out.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — command and control

isolate.title: Isolate (host isolation)
isolate.definition: Pulling a suspect machine off the network (or into a tight VLAN) so malware cannot reach shares, peers, or C2.
isolate.context: Desk-first move when ransomware or worm behavior shows up.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — isolation / incident response

do_not_pay.title: Do not pay (ransomware)
do_not_pay.definition: Organizational stance: do not pay the ransom — payment funds crime, may not restore data, and is not a recovery plan.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — ransomware response concepts

offline_backup.title: Offline / immutable backup
offline_backup.definition: Backup copies that ransomware cannot reach or alter — offline media, immutable snapshots, or air-gapped stores.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — backups / ransomware recovery

antivirus.title: Antivirus / antimalware
antivirus.definition: Endpoint software that detects, blocks, quarantines, or removes known and suspicious malicious code.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — antivirus / antimalware

signature_detection.title: Signature-based detection
signature_detection.definition: Matching files or patterns against known malware fingerprints (hashes, byte patterns).
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — signature-based detection

heuristic.title: Heuristic detection
heuristic.definition: Detecting suspicious behavior or code traits even when the exact malware sample is new.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — heuristic / behavior-based detection

living_off_the_land.title: Living off the land
living_off_the_land.definition: Abusing built-in OS tools (PowerShell, WMI, scripts) so attacks blend in with admin work.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — living off the land / fileless

persistence.title: Persistence
persistence.definition: Techniques that keep malware running after reboot — startup entries, services, scheduled tasks, registry Run keys.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — persistence / malware characteristics

privilege_escalation.title: Privilege escalation
privilege_escalation.definition: Gaining higher rights than the initial foothold — user to admin, or admin to SYSTEM/kernel.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — privilege escalation

lateral_movement.title: Lateral movement
lateral_movement.definition: Spreading from one compromised host to others on the same network — shares, remote tools, stolen creds.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — lateral movement

removable_media.title: Removable media risk
removable_media.definition: USB sticks and other portable media as a malware delivery path — plug in, autorun or open, infect.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — removable media / physical vectors

edr.title: EDR
edr.definition: Endpoint detection and response — tooling that records process/network behavior and helps hunt or contain malware.

network_share.title: Network share
network_share.definition: Folder or drive published on the LAN that many PCs can reach — a common path for worm or ransomware spread.

malware_scan.title: Malware scan
malware_scan.definition: On-demand or scheduled check by antimalware/EDR that looks for known and suspicious code on a host.

process_list.title: Process list
process_list.definition: Running programs visible in Task Manager or EDR — odd names, odd parents, or odd CPU can be early clues.

hash.title: File hash
hash.definition: Fingerprint of a file (MD5/SHA) used to match known-bad samples or prove two files are identical.

social_engineering.title: Social engineering
social_engineering.definition: Manipulating people into revealing information or taking unsafe actions — trust and pressure instead of breaking crypto.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — social engineering techniques

phishing.title: Phishing
phishing.definition: Fraudulent messages (usually email) that trick users into clicking, opening, or giving up secrets.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — phishing

spear_phishing.title: Spear phishing
spear_phishing.definition: Targeted phishing aimed at a specific person or small group, customized with personal or role details.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — spear phishing

whaling.title: Whaling
whaling.definition: Phishing aimed at high-value targets such as executives or other senior decision-makers.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — whaling

vishing.title: Vishing
vishing.definition: Voice phishing — social engineering over phone or voice calls.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — vishing

smishing.title: Smishing
smishing.definition: SMS phishing — fraudulent texts that push links, codes, or urgent actions.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — smishing

phishing_url.title: Phishing URL
phishing_url.definition: A link designed to look legitimate while sending the victim to an attacker-controlled site.
phishing_url.context: Hover, expand, or check the real host before you click.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — indicators of phishing

spoofing.title: Spoofing
spoofing.definition: Faking a sender identity — display name, email address, caller ID, or site look — to appear trusted.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — spoofing / impersonation

impersonation.title: Impersonation
impersonation.definition: Pretending to be a trusted person or role (boss, IT, vendor, bank) to get compliance.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — impersonation

pretexting.title: Pretexting
pretexting.definition: Inventing a believable story or role to justify asking for information or access.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — pretexting

quid_pro_quo.title: Quid pro quo
quid_pro_quo.definition: Offering a benefit (help, gift, refund, free support) in exchange for information or a risky action.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — quid pro quo

tailgating.title: Tailgating
tailgating.definition: Following an authorized person through a door without badging yourself — exploiting politeness.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — tailgating

dumpster_diving.title: Dumpster diving
dumpster_diving.definition: Searching discarded paper or media for secrets — passwords, org charts, invoices, badges.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — dumpster diving

watering_hole.title: Watering hole
watering_hole.definition: Compromising a site a target group already trusts, then waiting for victims to visit.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — watering hole

influence_campaigns.title: Influence campaigns
influence_campaigns.definition: Coordinated efforts to shape opinions or behavior at scale — often mixing social pressure with deceptive content.
influence_campaigns.context: On the exam: social engineering at organizational or public scale, not just one inbox.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — influence campaigns

urgency.title: Urgency
urgency.definition: Pressure to act immediately so the victim skips verification.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — social engineering principles (urgency)

familiarity.title: Familiarity
familiarity.definition: Using known names, slang, or shared context so a request feels like it comes from 'someone like us.'
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — social engineering principles (familiarity)

authority.title: Authority
authority.definition: Claiming power (executive, IT admin, law enforcement, vendor) so people comply without checking.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — social engineering principles (authority)

scarcity.title: Scarcity
scarcity.definition: Claiming limited time, seats, or stock so the victim rushes a decision.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — social engineering principles (scarcity)

consensus.title: Consensus (social proof)
consensus.definition: Implying everyone else already complied — 'your teammates already clicked / updated / paid.'
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — social engineering principles (consensus / social proof)

bec.title: Business email compromise (BEC)
bec.definition: Fraud that hijacks or fakes business email threads — often to redirect payments or steal wire instructions.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — BEC / business email compromise

credential_harvesting.title: Credential harvesting
credential_harvesting.definition: Collecting usernames and passwords (or tokens) via fake login pages or forms.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — phishing / credential harvesting

malware_attachment.title: Malware attachment
malware_attachment.definition: A file (or archive) delivered to install malware when opened — often paired with a urgent story.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — malicious attachments / phishing

typo_squatting.title: Typosquatting
typo_squatting.definition: Registering lookalike domains with typos or near-miss spellings of a trusted brand.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — typosquatting / URL indicators

brand_impersonation.title: Brand impersonation
brand_impersonation.definition: Copying logos, themes, and wording of a known company so a fake message or site feels official.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — brand impersonation / phishing indicators

hoax.title: Hoax
hoax.definition: A false warning or rumor spread to cause panic, wasted effort, or unsafe 'fixes.'
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — hoax

invoice_scam.title: Invoice scam
invoice_scam.definition: Fraudulent billing or payment-change request that looks like a normal vendor or finance workflow.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — invoice scams / BEC-related fraud

mfa_fatigue_attack.title: MFA fatigue attack
mfa_fatigue_attack.definition: Spamming MFA push prompts until the user approves one without thinking.
mfa_fatigue_attack.context: Same muscle as ch2 MFA habits — here it rides a phishing or password-spray path.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MFA / social engineering related attacks

reporting_path.title: Reporting path
reporting_path.definition: The official way to report suspected phishing or social engineering (button, mailbox, SOC, ticket) so response can start.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — reporting / incident awareness

mail_gateway.title: Mail gateway
mail_gateway.definition: Email security filter that scans, tags, quarantines, or blocks messages before they reach users.

user_reported.title: User-reported
user_reported.definition: Phish or suspicious message flagged by an employee (report button or forward) rather than only by automated filters.

phish_report_button.title: Phish report button
phish_report_button.definition: Client add-in that sends a suspected message to security for analysis without the user forwarding raw risk elsewhere.

sandbox.title: Sandbox
sandbox.definition: Isolated analysis environment where attachments or links can be opened safely for detonation checks.

physical_controls.title: Physical security controls
physical_controls.definition: Tangible barriers and processes that protect facilities, people, and hardware — fences, locks, cameras, badges, and the habits that make them work.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — physical security controls

fencing.title: Fencing
fencing.definition: Perimeter barrier that deters and delays casual entry — height, materials, and gates matter more than looking serious.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — fencing / perimeter

bollards.title: Bollards
bollards.definition: Short posts that stop or slow vehicles from ramming doors, glass, or loading docks.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — bollards

barricade.title: Barricade
barricade.definition: Temporary or permanent obstacle used to control vehicle or crowd movement around a site.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — barricades

lighting.title: Lighting (security)
lighting.definition: Illumination that reduces dark hiding spots and improves camera usefulness — a cheap control that attackers hate.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — lighting

industrial_camouflage.title: Industrial camouflage
industrial_camouflage.definition: Making a facility blend into the neighborhood so it draws less attention as a high-value target.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — industrial camouflage

signage.title: Signage
signage.definition: Posted notices that warn, direct, or mark restricted areas — supporting control, not a substitute for locks.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — signage

cctv.title: CCTV / cameras
cctv.definition: Video surveillance that records and deters — useful for investigation when retention and coverage are planned.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — cameras / CCTV

motion_detection.title: Motion detection
motion_detection.definition: Sensors that alert when movement occurs in a watched zone — often paired with cameras or alarms.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — motion detection

alarm_system.title: Alarm system
alarm_system.definition: Sensors and signaling that notify people of unauthorized entry, door forced open, or other physical events.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — alarms

security_guard.title: Security guard
security_guard.definition: Human presence that can challenge, escort, and respond — flexible where cameras only watch.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — security guards / personnel

reception.title: Reception / access desk
reception.definition: Front-desk checkpoint that verifies visitors, issues badges, and is the first human filter into the building.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — reception / access control personnel

access_badge.title: Access badge
access_badge.definition: Credential (card, fob, or phone token) presented to readers to open doors for authorized people.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — badges / access cards

proximity_card.title: Proximity / RFID badge
proximity_card.definition: Badge that unlocks when held near a reader — convenient, and clonable if not paired with PIN or biometrics.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — proximity cards / RFID

cable_lock.title: Cable lock
cable_lock.definition: Physical lock that tethers a laptop to furniture so walk-away theft is harder.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — cable locks

door_lock.title: Locks (doors)
door_lock.definition: Mechanical or electronic door hardware — deadbolts, electric strikes, cipher locks — that enforce who may enter.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — locks

mantrap.title: Mantrap
mantrap.definition: Two-door vestibule that only opens one door at a time so people cannot slip through with someone else.
mantrap.context: Also called an access control vestibule on some exams.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — mantrap / access control vestibule

secure_area.title: Secure area
secure_area.definition: Restricted space (server room, wiring closet, records vault) with stronger controls than the open floor.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — secure areas

visitor_log.title: Visitor log
visitor_log.definition: Record of who entered, when, and who escorted them — accountability for guests and contractors.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — visitor logs / escorts

clean_desk.title: Clean desk policy
clean_desk.definition: Requirement to clear sensitive papers and lock screens when leaving a workstation — no leftover secrets on the blotter.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — clean desk

privacy_filter.title: Privacy / screen filter
privacy_filter.definition: Overlay that narrows the viewing angle so neighbors and café eyes cannot easily read the display.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — privacy screens / filters

piggybacking.title: Piggybacking
piggybacking.definition: Entering with consent of the person who opened the door — they held it; you still did not authenticate.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — piggybacking

usb_data_blocker.title: USB data blocker
usb_data_blocker.definition: Inline adapter that passes power only — blocks data lines so a public charge port cannot talk to the phone.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — USB data blockers

faraday_cage.title: Faraday cage / bag
faraday_cage.definition: Conductive enclosure that blocks RF — used for evidence phones, test devices, or shielding sensitive gear.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — Faraday cages / bags

air_gap.title: Air gap
air_gap.definition: Keeping a system physically isolated from other networks — no cable, no Wi-Fi, no convenient USB bridge.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — air gap

protected_distribution.title: Protected cable distribution
protected_distribution.definition: Hardened or monitored pathways for sensitive cabling so taps and tampering are harder.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — protected cable distribution

hot_aisle.title: Hot / cold aisle (awareness)
hot_aisle.definition: Data-center layout that separates hot exhaust and cold intake — operational design that also shapes who can walk where.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — hot/cold aisle (physical / environmental)

badge_reader.title: Badge reader
badge_reader.definition: Door hardware that accepts a badge or PIN and signals the lock to open when policy allows.

server_room.title: Server room
server_room.definition: Secure area housing critical compute and network gear — usually badge-plus and camera-covered.

facilities.title: Facilities
facilities.definition: Building ops team that owns doors, cameras, lighting, and badge hardware alongside IT policy.

lobby.title: Lobby
lobby.definition: Public-facing entry where visitors meet reception — highest tailgating risk zone.

escort.title: Escort
escort.definition: Authorized person who accompanies a visitor in restricted space so guests are never unattended.

port.title: Port
port.definition: A 16-bit number (0–65535) that multiplexes traffic to a specific service or process on a host.

protocol.title: Protocol
protocol.definition: A formal set of message formats and rules that networked systems use to exchange data.

tcp.title: TCP
tcp.definition: Connection-oriented transport that sequences and acknowledges data so lost packets can be recovered.

udp.title: UDP
udp.definition: Connectionless transport that sends datagrams without guaranteed delivery; used when speed or simplicity matters more than recovery.

cleartext.title: Cleartext
cleartext.definition: Data sent without encryption so anyone on the path can read or alter it, including credentials.

http.title: HTTP (80/TCP)
http.definition: Cleartext web protocol. Replaced in production by HTTPS.

ftp.title: FTP (20/21/TCP)
ftp.definition: File transfer with cleartext commands and credentials. Port 21 is control; 20 is active-mode data. Replace with SFTP or FTPS.

sftp.title: SFTP (22/TCP)
sftp.definition: File transfer tunneled inside SSH. Different protocol from FTP; uses port 22, not 20/21.
sftp.context: Not the same as FTPS — file transfer inside SSH, usually port 22.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — secure file transfer alternatives to FTP

ftps.title: FTPS (989/990/TCP)
ftps.definition: FTP wrapped in TLS (implicit mode commonly 990 control / 989 data). Not the same as SFTP.
ftps.context: Classic FTP wrapped in TLS; different ports and firewall story than SFTP.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — secure file transfer alternatives to FTP

telnet.title: Telnet (23/TCP)
telnet.definition: Remote shell that sends everything — including passwords — in cleartext. Replace with SSH.
telnet.context: Do not allow on management paths; replace with SSH.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — insecure protocols / secure alternatives

ssh.title: SSH (22/TCP)
ssh.definition: Encrypted remote shell and tunnel. Also carries SFTP and SCP. The standard Telnet replacement.
ssh.context: Secure replacement for cleartext Telnet on remote admin paths.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — implement secure protocols (remote access)

smtp.title: SMTP (25/TCP)
smtp.definition: Server-to-server mail relay, historically cleartext. Clients should submit on 587 or 465 instead.

smtp_submission.title: SMTP submission (587/TCP)
smtp_submission.definition: Authenticated client mail submission, typically upgraded with STARTTLS. Modern send port.

smtps.title: SMTPS (465/TCP)
smtps.definition: SMTP wrapped in TLS from the first byte (implicit TLS).

pop3.title: POP3 (110/TCP)
pop3.definition: Downloads mail to the client in cleartext. Secure version is POP3S on 995.

imap.title: IMAP (143/TCP)
imap.definition: Server-side mailbox access in cleartext. Secure version is IMAPS on 993.

imaps.title: IMAPS (993/TCP)
imaps.definition: IMAP wrapped in TLS — keeps mail on the server with encryption in transit.

dns.title: DNS (53/UDP/TCP)
dns.definition: Resolves names to addresses. UDP 53 for normal lookups; TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses. Classic DNS is unencrypted.

dhcp.title: DHCP (67/68/UDP)
dhcp.definition: Assigns IP configuration. Server listens on 67; client on 68.

ntp.title: NTP (123/UDP)
ntp.definition: Synchronizes clocks. Accurate time matters for logs, Kerberos tickets, and certificate validation.

ldap.title: LDAP (389/TCP/UDP)
ldap.definition: Directory lookups and authentication in cleartext. Secure version is LDAPS on 636.

ldaps.title: LDAPS (636/TCP)
ldaps.context: Directory binds with passwords should not ride cleartext LDAP on untrusted segments.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — implement secure protocols (directory services)

kerberos.title: Kerberos (88/TCP/UDP)
kerberos.definition: Ticket-based authentication used by Active Directory. Issues time-limited tickets instead of sending reusable passwords repeatedly.

snmp.title: SNMP (161/162/UDP)
snmp.definition: Device monitoring. 161 polls agents; 162 receives traps. v1/v2c send community strings in cleartext — prefer SNMPv3.

snmpv3.title: SNMPv3
snmpv3.definition: SNMP with authentication and encryption. Same ports as classic SNMP, but credentials are no longer cleartext community strings.

syslog.title: Syslog (514/UDP)
syslog.definition: Cleartext log forwarding to a collector. Secure with syslog over TLS on 6514.

syslog_tls.title: Syslog over TLS (6514/TCP)
syslog_tls.definition: Syslog carried inside TLS so log data stays confidential and intact in transit.

smb.title: SMB (445/TCP)
smb.definition: Windows file and printer sharing. Never expose to the Internet; a frequent worm and ransomware path.

rdp.title: RDP (3389/TCP)
rdp.definition: Microsoft Remote Desktop. Encrypted in modern use, but Internet-exposed RDP is a leading ransomware entry — keep it behind a VPN.
rdp.context: Do not expose raw 3389 to the internet; prefer VPN then jump host.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — firewall ports/protocols; secure remote access

radius.title: RADIUS
radius.definition: Authentication server protocol commonly behind enterprise Wi-Fi — checks user/device credentials for 802.1X.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — RADIUS / AAA

tacacs.title: TACACS+ (49/TCP)
tacacs.definition: Cisco AAA protocol that encrypts the full payload and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting.

tftp.title: TFTP (69/UDP)
tftp.definition: Tiny file transfer with no authentication. Acceptable only on trusted networks for device configs or PXE — never across a perimeter.

firewall_rule.title: Firewall rule (ports/protocols)
firewall_rule.definition: An allow or deny decision keyed to source, destination, port, and protocol — the operational place Security+ port knowledge gets used.

msp.title: MSP
msp.definition: Managed Service Provider; a company that runs IT support for other businesses.

vlan.title: VLAN
vlan.definition: Virtual LAN; a logical network segment that isolates traffic without separate physical wiring.

enable_password.title: Enable password
enable_password.definition: Privileged password on network gear that unlocks administrative (enable) mode.

key_auth.title: Key authentication
key_auth.definition: Logging in with a cryptographic key pair instead of (or in addition to) a password.

starttls.title: STARTTLS
starttls.definition: A command that upgrades an existing cleartext connection to TLS mid-session (common on mail submission).
starttls.context: Upgrades an existing cleartext mail session mid-stream (common on submission port 587).

open_relay.title: Open relay
open_relay.definition: A mail server that accepts and forwards mail from anyone; abused by spammers.

jump_host.title: Jump host / jump box
jump_host.definition: A hardened intermediate server you remote into first, then reach internal systems from there.
jump_host.context: Intermediate hop so workstations are not directly reachable from remote clients.

vpn.title: VPN
vpn.definition: Encrypted tunnel for traffic — still wise on untrusted Wi-Fi even when the café page looks friendly.

directory_bind.title: Directory bind
directory_bind.definition: An application authenticating/connecting to a directory service (like LDAP) to look up or validate accounts.

domain.title: Domain
domain.definition: An administrative realm (often Active Directory) that shares authentication and policy.

dhcp_lease.title: DHCP lease
dhcp_lease.definition: Temporary IP configuration handed out by DHCP for a limited time.

resolver_cache.title: Resolver cache
resolver_cache.definition: Local store of recent DNS answers; flushing it forces fresh lookups.

community_string.title: Community string
community_string.definition: A shared secret in SNMPv1/v2c that acts like a password and is sent in cleartext.

aaa.title: AAA
aaa.definition: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting — proving identity, deciding what you may do, and logging what you did.

authz.title: Authorization (authz)
authz.definition: What an authenticated user or device is allowed to do (distinct from authentication).

concentrator.title: VPN concentrator
concentrator.definition: Device/service that terminates many VPN tunnels for remote users.

perimeter.title: Network perimeter
perimeter.definition: Boundary between trusted internal networks and untrusted external networks.

guest_wifi.title: Guest Wi-Fi
guest_wifi.definition: Separate wireless access for visitors — should not freely reach internal servers or employee laptops.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — guest network

implicit_tls.title: Implicit TLS
implicit_tls.definition: Wrapping a protocol in TLS from the first byte (e.g. SMTPS 465, FTPS 990) rather than upgrading mid-session with STARTTLS.

change_ticket.title: Change (change ticket)
change_ticket.definition: Tracked request to modify production systems (firewall rules, certs, configs) with review/approval.

firewall.title: Firewall
firewall.definition: Device or software that allows or denies traffic based on rules (addresses, ports, protocols).

ssid.title: SSID
ssid.definition: Service set identifier — the network name a wireless network advertises (or tries to hide).
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — SSID / wireless basics

wep.title: WEP
wep.definition: Wired Equivalent Privacy — obsolete Wi-Fi encryption that is easily broken; treat as insecure legacy.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — WEP (insecure)

wpa2.title: WPA2
wpa2.definition: Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 — widely deployed Wi-Fi security using strong encryption (AES-CCMP) when configured correctly.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — WPA2

wpa3.title: WPA3
wpa3.definition: Newer Wi-Fi security standard with stronger protections (including SAE) against offline password attacks and better open-network options.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — WPA3

sae.title: SAE
sae.definition: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals — WPA3 handshake that resists offline dictionary attacks better than WPA2-PSK.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — WPA3 / SAE

psk.title: PSK (pre-shared key)
psk.definition: Shared Wi-Fi password mode — everyone uses the same key; fine for small spaces, weak for accountability and rotation.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — PSK / personal mode

enterprise_wpa.title: WPA-Enterprise (802.1X)
enterprise_wpa.definition: Wi-Fi that authenticates each user/device via 802.1X (usually RADIUS) instead of one shared password.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise / 802.1X

ieee_8021x.title: 802.1X
ieee_8021x.definition: Port-based network access control — authenticate before full network access; used for enterprise Wi-Fi and wired NAC.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — 802.1X

open_network.title: Open network
open_network.definition: Wi-Fi with no encryption on the air — anyone nearby can join and often eavesdrop unless a higher layer protects traffic.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — open / insecure wireless

captive_portal.title: Captive portal
captive_portal.definition: Web login/splash page before internet access — common on guest Wi-Fi; not a substitute for strong link encryption by itself.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — captive portal / guest access

wps.title: WPS
wps.definition: Wi-Fi Protected Setup — convenience pairing feature with a history of brute-force weaknesses; disable when possible.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — WPS risks

evil_twin.title: Evil twin
evil_twin.definition: Attacker access point that mimics a trusted SSID to trick clients into connecting and exposing traffic or credentials.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — evil twin

rogue_ap.title: Rogue access point
rogue_ap.definition: Unauthorized AP on the network or in range — intentional attack gear or a well-meaning employee 'helping' coverage.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — rogue access point

disassociation.title: Disassociation / deauthentication
disassociation.definition: Wireless frames that kick clients off an AP — used in DoS or to force reconnects toward an evil twin.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — disassociation / deauthentication attacks

jamming.title: Jamming
jamming.definition: Flooding RF so legitimate Wi-Fi cannot communicate — a denial-of-service against the air itself.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — jamming / RF interference (attack)

war_driving.title: War driving
war_driving.definition: Roaming an area to discover and map Wi-Fi networks — often looking for weak or open targets.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — war driving

eavesdropping.title: Wireless eavesdropping
eavesdropping.definition: Capturing Wi-Fi frames from the air — catastrophic on open/WEP, still a concern if clients join the wrong network.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — eavesdropping / sniffing

replay_attack.title: Replay attack
replay_attack.definition: Capturing valid wireless or auth traffic and re-sending it later to gain access or disrupt sessions.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — replay attacks

iv_attack.title: IV attack (WEP)
iv_attack.definition: Exploiting WEP's weak initialization vectors to recover the key — one reason WEP is retired.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — IV attack / WEP weaknesses

site_survey.title: Site survey
site_survey.definition: Measuring coverage, interference, and dead zones so APs are placed and tuned for both performance and security boundaries.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — site survey

segmentation.title: Network segmentation
segmentation.definition: Splitting networks so a compromise or guest device cannot freely reach sensitive systems.
segmentation.context: Guest Wi-Fi without segmentation is a hallway into the building.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — network segmentation

hidden_ssid.title: Hidden SSID
hidden_ssid.definition: Not broadcasting the network name — weak obscurity; determined clients and attackers can still discover it.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — SSID suppression

mac_filtering.title: MAC filtering
mac_filtering.definition: Allow/deny Wi-Fi by hardware address — easily spoofed; not a real access-control substitute.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — MAC filtering

ap_placement.title: AP placement
ap_placement.definition: Where access points sit and how loud they transmit — affects coverage, leakage outside the building, and attack surface.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — access point placement / power levels

wifi_analyzer.title: Wi-Fi analyzer
wifi_analyzer.definition: Tool that shows SSIDs, channels, signal strength, and sometimes security modes — useful for survey and spotting twins.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — wireless analyzers / site survey tools

bluetooth.title: Bluetooth
bluetooth.definition: Short-range wireless for peripherals and phones — convenient, and a side channel if pairing is careless.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — Bluetooth risks

bluejacking.title: Bluejacking
bluejacking.definition: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices — annoying spam more than full takeover.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — bluejacking

bluesnarfing.title: Bluesnarfing
bluesnarfing.definition: Unauthorized access to data on a Bluetooth device — contacts, messages, files — when pairing/security is weak.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — bluesnarfing

bluetooth_pairing.title: Bluetooth pairing hygiene
bluetooth_pairing.definition: Only pair expected devices, prefer confirm codes, turn discovery off when idle — desk-level Bluetooth risk control.
refs: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — Bluetooth security practices

access_point.title: Access point (AP)
access_point.definition: Device that bridges wireless clients onto the wired LAN — the radio end of corporate Wi-Fi.

controller.title: Wireless controller
controller.definition: Central brain that manages many APs — SSIDs, encryption mode, rogue detection, guest policy.

signal_strength.title: Signal strength
signal_strength.definition: How loud the AP looks to a client — useful for coverage tickets and for noticing a twin that is 'too strong' in the wrong place.

vlan_trunking.title: VLAN Trunking (802.1Q)
vlan_trunking.definition: A Layer 2 bridging mechanism allowing multiple virtual local area networks to traverse a single physical link by inserting a 4-byte 802.1Q VLAN tag into the Ethernet frame header.
vlan_trunking.context: Carries isolated traffic classes—including Corporate, Telemetry, and VoIP—across campus backbone links without requiring dedicated physical cables for each broadcast domain.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 2.1 — Configure and apply switching features (VLANs, 802.1Q trunking, native VLAN)
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 2.1 — Network switching concepts and inter-VLAN transport

dhcp_exhaustion.title: DHCP Scope Exhaustion
dhcp_exhaustion.definition: A network denial-of-service condition where a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol scope has leased all available IP addresses in its configured allocation pool, preventing new or reconnecting devices from acquiring valid Layer 3 network parameters.
dhcp_exhaustion.context: Forces booting clients into APIPA link-local addresses (169.254.x.x); commonly occurs when massive device reconnect storms collide with excessively long lease durations.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.4 & 4.1 — IPv4 addressing, DHCP pools, and troubleshooting IP assignment
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 4.1 — Troubleshooting common network service failures

patch_panel.title: Patch Panel
patch_panel.definition: A passive, rack-mounted structural interconnect device containing female RJ-45 modular jacks on the front faceplate and 110-style insulation displacement contact punchdown blocks on the rear to terminate horizontal structured cabling.
patch_panel.context: Protects fragile horizontal solid-core cabling from mechanical wear and tear by allowing technicians to cross-connect ports using flexible stranded patch cables.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 1.2 — Cable management, patch panels, punchdown blocks, and Layer 1 physical infrastructure
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 1.2 — Physical media and structured cabling distribution

flea_power.title: Flea Power (Residual Energy)
flea_power.definition: The residual static electrical charge stored in motherboard capacitors, power supply filter stages, and integrated circuits after primary electrical power is disconnected.
flea_power.context: Must be fully discharged by disconnecting power cords and depressing the power button for thirty seconds to clear corrupt memory registers before replacing hardware.
refs: CompTIA A+ Core 1 220-1101 Domain 3.0 — Hardware break/fix and power triage
CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 4.1 — Physical hardware troubleshooting methodology

spanning_tree.title: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP / 802.1D / 802.1w)
spanning_tree.definition: A Layer 2 network protocol that monitors bridge topology and dynamically places redundant switch ports into blocking state to prevent catastrophic broadcast storms and switching loops.
spanning_tree.context: Transitions ports through listening, learning, and forwarding states (or rapid sync) to ensure a single, loop-free active path exists across redundant campus switches.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 2.1 — Switching features, loop prevention, and Spanning Tree Protocol
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 2.1 — Layer 2 protocols and high-availability switching

link_aggregation.title: Link Aggregation (LACP / 802.3ad)
link_aggregation.definition: A networking standard (Link Aggregation Control Protocol) that bundles multiple physical Ethernet interfaces into a single logical channel to provide multiplied bandwidth and active-active hardware redundancy.
link_aggregation.context: Protects critical inter-switch uplinks against single-cable failures while preventing Spanning Tree Protocol from blocking the parallel physical links.
refs: CompTIA Network+ N10-008 Domain 2.1 — Port bonding, link aggregation, and LACP
CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Domain 2.1 — High availability, trunking, and NIC teaming
